title: Breadth: the market's X-ray
teaches: Read what the index can hide: the advance/decline line, the share of stocks above their 50-day and 200-day averages, new 52-week highs against new lows, and the McClellan Oscillator, and treat a breadth divergence as a warning, not a timing signal.

facts.quote: Breadth indicators measure the number or percentage of stocks in the group that are participating in a trend.
facts.claim: Breadth gauges count how many stocks in a group are taking part in a trend.

facts.quote: The Advance-Decline Line (AD Line) is a breadth indicator based on Net Advances, which is the number of advancing stocks less the number of declining stocks.
facts.claim: Net advances are advancing stocks minus declining stocks, and the A/D line is built from them.

facts.quote: The AD Line is a cumulative measure of Net Advances, rising when it is positive and falling when it is negative.
facts.claim: The A/D line is a running total of net advances: it rises on positive days and falls on negative ones.

facts.quote: Subsequent values are calculated using the AD Line value for the previous period's value plus Net Advances for the current period.
facts.claim: Today's A/D line is yesterday's value plus today's net advances.

facts.quote: The actual value of the AD Line depends on the starting point for the calculation.
facts.claim: The A/D line's number depends on the day you start counting.

facts.quote: The shape and direction of the AD Line are important, not the actual value.
facts.claim: Read the A/D line's shape and direction, not its level.

facts.quote: An AD Line that rises and records new highs along with the underlying index shows strong participation that is bullish.
facts.claim: An A/D line making new highs with its index shows strong, bullish participation.

facts.quote: An AD Line that fails to keep pace with the underlying index and confirm new highs shows narrowing participation.
facts.claim: An A/D line that fails to confirm the index's new highs shows narrowing participation.

facts.quote: Narrowing participation is often identified with a bearish divergence between the AD Line and the underlying index.
facts.claim: Narrowing participation often shows up as a bearish divergence between the A/D line and its index.

facts.quote: A bullish divergence forms when the AD Line fails to record a lower low along with the index. This means fewer stocks are declining and the decline in the index may be nearing an end.
facts.claim: Bullish divergence: the index makes a lower low and the A/D line does not, so fewer stocks are falling and the decline may be ending.

facts.quote: Chart 3 shows two bearish divergences in the NYSE AD Line from June to November 2007. The NYSE Composite moved to new highs in July, but the AD Line peaked at the beginning of June.
facts.claim: In 2007 the NYSE A/D line peaked in early June while the NYSE Composite went on to new highs in July.

facts.quote: The NYSE Composite surged again to new highs in October, but the AD Line fell well short of its July high and formed another bearish divergence in October.
facts.claim: In October 2007 the NYSE Composite made new highs again while the A/D line stayed well below its July high.

facts.quote: This string of bearish divergences foreshadowed the January support break and the bear market of 2008.
facts.claim: Those 2007 divergences came before the January support break and the 2008 bear market.

facts.quote: First, the Nasdaq AD Line can fall for extended periods, even if the Nasdaq itself is rising. This is because Nasdaq listing requirements are not as strict as NYSE listing requirements.
facts.claim: The Nasdaq A/D line can fall for long periods while the Nasdaq rises, because Nasdaq's listing rules are looser.

facts.quote: Chart 4 shows the Nasdaq AD Line declining even as the Nasdaq advanced from 2010 until 2012.
facts.claim: From 2010 to 2012 the Nasdaq A/D line fell while the Nasdaq rose.

facts.quote: Second, the advance-decline statistics favor small-cap and mid-cap stocks over large-cap stocks.
facts.claim: Advance-decline numbers lean toward small and mid caps, not large caps.

facts.quote: Thousands of stocks trade on the Nasdaq and NYSE every day and the vast majority of these stocks are small- and mid-cap. Relatively few are large-caps.
facts.claim: Most stocks trading each day are small and mid caps; few are large caps.

facts.quote: Regardless of market cap or volume, an advance counts as +1 and a decline counts as -1.
facts.claim: Every advancing stock counts +1 and every declining stock -1, whatever its size or volume.

facts.quote: A broad-based advance shows underlying strength that lifts most boats. This is bullish.
facts.claim: A broad advance that lifts most stocks is bullish.

facts.quote: For short-to-medium-term timeframes, it's helpful to look at the percentage of stocks trading above the 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: For short to medium-term views, watch the share of stocks above their 50-day average.

facts.quote: For medium-to-long-term-timeframes, it's best to look at the percentage of stocks trading above the 150-day and 200-day moving averages.
facts.claim: For medium to long-term views, watch the share above the 150-day and 200-day averages.

facts.quote: The calculation is straightforward: divide the number of stocks above their XX-day moving average by the total number of stocks in the underlying index.
facts.claim: Percent above = stocks above the average divided by all stocks in the index.

facts.quote: A bullish bias is present when the indicator is above 50%. This means more than half the stocks in the index are above a particular moving average. A bearish bias is present when below 50%.
facts.claim: Above 50% gives a bullish bias (most stocks above their average); below 50% gives a bearish bias.

facts.quote: The percent of stocks above their 50-day moving average is more volatile and crosses the 50% threshold more often.
facts.claim: The 50-day version swings more and crosses 50% more often than the longer ones.

facts.quote: In general, readings above 70% are deemed overbought and readings below 30% are deemed oversold. These levels may vary for other indices.
facts.claim: ChartSchool treats above 70% as overbought and below 30% as oversold, and says the levels vary by index.

facts.quote: Just like momentum oscillators, this indicator can become overbought numerous times in a strong uptrend or oversold many times during a strong downtrend.
facts.claim: In a strong trend this gauge can go overbought (uptrend) or oversold (downtrend) again and again.

facts.quote: With an overall uptrend in progress, overbought conditions were ignored and oversold conditions were used as buying opportunities.
facts.claim: In ChartSchool's uptrend example, overbought readings were ignored and oversold dips were used as buying chances.

facts.quote: Multiple overbought readings are a sign of strength, not weakness.
facts.claim: Repeated overbought readings are a sign of strength, not weakness.

facts.quote: Simply becoming oversold is not always a buy signal. It is often prudent to wait for an upturn from oversold levels.
facts.claim: Oversold alone is not always a buy signal; it is often wiser to wait for an upturn.

facts.quote: With the bigger trend down, oversold conditions were ignored and overbought conditions were used as selling alerts.
facts.claim: In ChartSchool's downtrend example, oversold readings were ignored and overbought bounces were the selling alerts.

facts.quote: Net New 52-Week Highs is a simple breadth indicator found by subtracting new lows from new highs.
facts.claim: Net new highs are new highs minus new lows.

facts.quote: “New lows” is the number of stocks recording new 52-week lows. “New highs” is the number of stocks making new 52-week highs.
facts.claim: New highs and new lows count stocks at 52-week highs and 52-week lows.

facts.quote: There are more new highs when the indicator is positive, which favors the bulls. There are more new lows when the indicator is negative, which favors the bears.
facts.claim: More new highs than lows favors the bulls; more new lows favors the bears.

facts.quote: New highs and new lows often lag the underlying index at major turning points. In other words, the market will change direction one to three months before there is a significant shift in new highs and new lows.
facts.claim: New highs and lows lag at major turns: the market often turns one to three months before they shift.

facts.quote: Chart 2 below shows the NY Composite ($NYA) with NYSE Net New Highs ($NYHL) in 2009.
facts.claim: ChartSchool's example tracks the NYSE Composite and NYSE net new highs through 2009.

facts.quote: The NY Composite bottomed in early March and moved sharply higher until early June. Despite this strong advance, Net New Highs did not increase significantly.
facts.claim: The NYSE Composite bottomed in early March 2009 and rallied hard into June, yet net new highs barely rose.

facts.quote: Net New Highs did not increase until mid-July and did not exceed +100 until August.
facts.claim: Net new highs did not rise until mid-July 2009 and did not top +100 until August.

facts.quote: Record High Percent = {New Highs / (New Highs + New Lows)} x 100
facts.claim: Record High Percent is new highs divided by new highs plus new lows, times 100.

facts.quote: Readings below 50 indicate that there were more new lows than new highs. Readings above 50 indicate that there were more new highs than new lows.
facts.claim: Below 50, new lows outnumber new highs; above 50, new highs outnumber new lows.

facts.quote: This indicator can move to its extremities and remain near its extremes when the underlying index is in a strong uptrend or downtrend.
facts.claim: In a strong trend this gauge can stay near its extremes.

facts.quote: Chartists can focus on bearish signals when the High-Low Index trades below 50 and ignore bullish signals.
facts.claim: Below 50, ChartSchool's approach is to favor bearish signals and set bullish ones aside.

facts.quote: Armed with a bullish or bearish bias, chartists can then turn to other aspects of technical analysis to generate corresponding signals.
facts.claim: Breadth gives the bias; the chart gives the signals.

facts.quote: Developed by Sherman and Marian McClellan, the McClellan Oscillator is a breadth indicator derived from Net Advances, which is the number of advancing issues less the number of declining issues.
facts.claim: Sherman and Marian McClellan built the McClellan Oscillator from net advances.

facts.quote: Subtracting the 39-day exponential moving average of Net Advances from the 19-day exponential moving average of Net Advances forms the oscillator.
facts.claim: The McClellan Oscillator is the 19-day EMA of net advances minus the 39-day EMA.

facts.quote: As the formula reveals, the McClellan Oscillator is a momentum indicator that works similar to Moving Average Convergence/Divergence (MACD).
facts.claim: The McClellan Oscillator is a momentum gauge that works like MACD.

facts.quote: The McClellan Oscillator is positive when the 19-day EMA (shorter moving average) is above the 39-day (longer moving average) EMA. This signals that advances are gaining the upper hand.
facts.claim: When the 19-day EMA is above the 39-day EMA the oscillator is positive: advancing stocks are gaining the upper hand.

facts.quote: Typically, the indicator will move from below -50 and exceed +50 for a +100 point thrust. A breadth thrust signals a surge in bullish breadth that can lead to an extended advance.
facts.claim: A typical breadth thrust runs from below -50 to above +50, a 100-point surge that can start an extended advance.

facts.quote: Not all breadth thrusts foreshadow extended advances, but most important lows are marked by a sharp surge in breadth.
facts.claim: Not every thrust leads to a big run, but most important lows show a sharp surge in breadth.

facts.quote: There will be many divergences and most will not result in reversals or extended moves.
facts.claim: McClellan Oscillator divergences are common, and most do not lead to reversals.

facts.quote: Like MACD, the McClellan Oscillator is a rather volatile indicator that produces many potential signals. Signals should be confirmed or refuted with other technical indicators and chart analysis.
facts.claim: The oscillator is volatile and throws many signals; confirm them with the chart.

facts.quote: Market breadth refers to how many stocks are participating in a given move in an index or on a stock exchange.
facts.claim: Market breadth is how many stocks take part in a move.

facts.quote: An index may be rising yet more than half the stocks in the index are falling because a small number of stocks have such large gains that they drag the whole index higher.
facts.claim: A few big gainers can lift an index while more than half its stocks fall.

facts.quote: Certain breadth indicators also incorporate volume.
facts.claim: Some breadth gauges also use volume.

facts.quote: Market breadth indicators are poor timing signals. They may provide signals way too early or may not forecast an index reversal that does occur.
facts.claim: Breadth gauges time poorly: they can warn far too early or miss a reversal.

facts.quote: A good rule of thumb is to never base trading decisions on what the indicator is saying. Always confirm with price.
facts.claim: Don't trade on a breadth reading alone; confirm with price.

facts.quote: Market depth, on the other hand, is a market's ability to handle relatively large orders without significantly impacting the price of a security.
facts.claim: Market depth is a different idea: how much size the market takes without moving the price much.

facts.quote: Short-term traders who want a more sensitive moving average to provide earlier signals can use a 50-day index that shows what percentage of stocks are trading above their 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: The share above the 50-day is the more sensitive, earlier gauge for short-term traders.

facts.quote: The advance/decline line (or A/D line) is a technical indicator that plots the difference between the number of advancing and declining stocks on a daily basis.
facts.claim: The A/D line plots advancing minus declining stocks each day.

facts.quote: The indicator is cumulative, with a positive number being added to the prior number, or if the number is negative it is subtracted from the prior number.
facts.claim: The A/D line is cumulative: each day's net number is added to the prior total.

facts.quote: If the indexes are moving up but the A/D line is sloping downwards, called bearish divergence, it's a sign that the markets are losing their breadth and may be about to reverse direction.
facts.claim: Index up while the A/D line slopes down is a bearish divergence: breadth is weakening.

facts.quote: Conversely, if the indexes are continuing to move lower and the A/D line has turned upwards, called bullish divergence, it may be an indication that the sellers are losing their conviction.
facts.claim: Index down while the A/D line turns up is a bullish divergence: sellers may be losing conviction.

facts.quote: Because of this, the A/D line will sometimes fall for extended periods of time, even while NASDAQ-related indexes are rising.
facts.claim: The Nasdaq A/D line can fall for long periods while Nasdaq indexes rise.

facts.quote: Another thing to be aware of is that some indexes are market capitalization weighted. This means that the bigger the company the more impact they have on the index's movement.
facts.claim: In a cap-weighted index, bigger companies move the index more.

facts.quote: The A/D line gives equal weight to all stocks. Therefore, it is a better gauge of the average small to mid-cap stock, and not the fewer in number large or mega-cap stocks.
facts.claim: The A/D line weights every stock equally, so it tracks the average small and mid cap, not the giants.

facts.quote: The indicator is positive when the 19-day EMA is above the 39-day EMA, and negative when the 19-day EMA is below the 39-day EMA.
facts.claim: The McClellan Oscillator is positive when the 19-day EMA is above the 39-day EMA, negative when below.

facts.quote: When the indicator makes a large move, typically of 100 points or more, from negative to positive territory, that is called a breadth thrust.
facts.claim: A large move from negative to positive, typically 100 points or more, is called a breadth thrust.

facts.quote: The McClellan Oscillator was developed by Sherman and Marian McClellan, who also developed the McClellan Summation Index.
facts.claim: Sherman and Marian McClellan developed the oscillator and the Summation Index.

facts.quote: The indicator is prone to producing false signals and therefore should be used in conjunction with price action analysis and other technical indicators.
facts.claim: The oscillator gives false signals, so use it with price action.

facts.quote: A high-low index above 50 means more stocks are reaching 52-week highs than reaching 52 lows. Conversely, a reading below 50 shows that more stocks are making 52-week lows compared to stocks making 52-week highs.
facts.claim: Above 50, more stocks are at 52-week highs than lows; below 50, more are at lows.

facts.quote: The high-low index is simply a 10-day moving average of the record high percent indicator, which divides new highs by new highs plus new lows.
facts.claim: The record high percent divides new highs by new highs plus new lows.

facts.quote: Investors should also be aware that If the market is trending strongly, the high-low index can give extreme readings for a prolonged period.
facts.claim: In a strong trend the high-low index can stay at an extreme for a long time.

facts.quote: For instance, if the indicator is above 50, a trader may decide to trade on the long side of the market only.
facts.claim: Above 50, a trader may choose to trade only the long side.

facts.quote: Breadth indicators don't typically provide trade signals on their own, but rather provide an overall picture of the health on an index.
facts.claim: Breadth shows the health of the market; on its own it is not a trade signal.

facts.quote: Trends can last a very long time on decreasing volume or even decreasing stock participation, which will lead to the breadth indicators diverging but not necessarily resulting in a price reversal.
facts.claim: Trends can run a long time on shrinking participation; a divergence doesn't always end in a reversal.

facts.quote: For example, if the Advance/Decline Line starts to drop while the S&P 500 is still rising, traders will watch closely for the S&P 500 to break below a rising trendline, break below support
facts.claim: When the A/D line drops while the index still rises, watch price for a break of its trendline or support.

facts.quote: Breadth indicators won't always forewarn of a reversal.
facts.claim: Breadth won't always warn before a reversal.

facts.quote: Up/Down Volume Spread which is up volume minus down volume.
facts.claim: Up volume minus down volume is a separate, volume-based gauge.

facts.quote: A capitalization-weighted index gives weight to its components based on their market capitalizations, giving the largest companies more influence on its performance.
facts.claim: A cap-weighted index gives its largest companies the most influence.

facts.quote: If stocks or an index are rising but the A/D line is falling, fewer stocks are contributing to the rally and that could signal a potential reversal of the uptrend.
facts.claim: Index rising while the A/D line falls means fewer stocks are carrying the rally.

facts.quote: Since the Iran conflict selloff hit its most recent nadir in late March, the S&P 500's advance/decline line has been trending higher (see chart below) alongside the index itself—which once again recaptured 7,000.
facts.claim: From the late-March 2026 low, the S&P 500's A/D line rose alongside the index, which got back above 7,000.

facts.quote: Source: FactSet, as of April 16, 2026.
facts.claim: Fidelity's chart data runs to April 16, 2026.

facts.quote: The combination of the rising advance/decline line and the S&P 500's rally suggests investor sentiment is broadly bullish.
facts.claim: Fidelity read the rising A/D line together with the index rally as broadly bullish.

facts.quote: Of course, these signals may not always confirm trends or forecast potential reversals, but investors can use them to broadly assess investor sentiment.
facts.claim: A/D signals don't always confirm trends or call reversals.

facts.quote: The difference between these numbers is called the daily breadth. The running cumulative total of daily breadth is known as the Daily Advance-Decline Line.
facts.claim: Advances minus declines is the daily breadth; its running total is the A/D line.

facts.quote: The McClellan Oscillator and Summation Index were developed by my parents back in 1969.
facts.claim: Tom McClellan says his parents developed the oscillator and the Summation Index in 1969.

facts.quote: it pushed the DJIA and other indices to higher highs. But so far, the NYSE's A-D Line has not followed suit.
facts.claim: In December 2013 the Dow made higher highs and the NYSE A/D line did not.

facts.quote: But the A-D Line peaked on Oct. 29, 2013, and as of the close on Dec. 18, 2013, it is still 2700 increments below that October high.
facts.claim: The NYSE A/D line peaked on Oct. 29, 2013 and was still below that high on Dec. 18, 2013.

facts.quote: That sort of bearish divergence is not good news, although it does not necessarily have to bring the price uptrend to an immediate halt.
facts.claim: A bearish divergence is bad news, but it doesn't have to stop the uptrend right away.

facts.quote: The composite A-D Line peaked on June 4, 2007, just over 4 months ahead of the final top for the DJIA.
facts.claim: The NYSE A/D line peaked on June 4, 2007, just over 4 months before the Dow's final top.

facts.quote: It is only the last new high that is the bearish one, and along the way a lot of bullish new highs can pile up.
facts.claim: Only the last new high is the bearish one; many bullish new highs can come first.

facts.quote: The scaling of the numbers on the Y-axis is not important; it just reflects what has happened in the time since one's chosen start point for the data.
facts.claim: The A/D line's scale isn't important; it only reflects the chosen start date.

facts.quote: For now, though, the Fed is still pouring money in, and we still have the A-D Line making higher highs to say that liquidity is plentiful enough to lift the majority of issues.
facts.claim: By June 2014 the NYSE A/D line was making higher highs again.

facts.quote: Over most of the history of the A-D data (dating back to 1926), the answer is that the damage is usually limited to about a 10% max drawdown within the 3 months after a new A-D Line high.
facts.claim: McClellan's study: after a new A/D line high, the worst S&P 500 drop over the next 3 months was usually about 10% or less.

facts.quote: But just one month later, in July-August 2011, we saw a 19% drawdown in the SP500.
facts.claim: In July-August 2011 the S&P 500 fell 19%, a month after the A/D line was still showing strong liquidity.

facts.quote: This goes against the historic "rule" that a new A-D Line high provides immunity from anything worse than about a 10% drawdown.
facts.claim: 2011 broke the historic pattern that a new A/D line high limits the next drop to about 10%.

facts.quote: Most price indices are dominated by the largest capitalization stocks, but every stock gets an equal vote in the A-D Line.
facts.claim: Price indexes are dominated by the biggest stocks; on the A/D line every stock gets an equal vote.

facts.quote: Any divergence represents a "condition", and is not a "signal".
facts.claim: A divergence is a condition, not a signal.

facts.quote: Divergences can also sometimes get "rehabilitated". If these A-D Lines start moving up and making higher highs again, then the apparent divergences we see now go away.
facts.claim: If the A/D line goes on to make higher highs, the divergence goes away.

facts.quote: The Nasdaq Composite Index is currently making new all-time highs, but its A-D Line is near its all-time low readings. This is not unusual.
facts.claim: In June 2024 the Nasdaq Composite was at record highs while its A/D line sat near record lows, which McClellan called not unusual.

facts.quote: The listing standards for stocks are looser on the Nasdaq than on the NYSE. So a stock which is going to go from IPO to broke is more likely to be listed on the Nasdaq.
facts.claim: Nasdaq's looser listing standards mean more stocks that fail, and each one adds to the declines.

facts.quote: It started downward from the beginning of the data in 1972, and has never gotten back to that level.
facts.claim: The Nasdaq A/D line has fallen since its data began in 1972 and never got back to its starting level.

facts.quote: We have just seen a new all-time high in the NYSE's daily Advance-Decline (A-D) Line. It confirms the new highs in the major indices, and that is a really good thing.
facts.claim: In January 2026 the NYSE A/D line made a new all-time high, confirming the indexes' new highs.

facts.quote: We also had a big exception to the rule about new A-D Line highs back in 2020, when the arrival of Covid into the US led to a government shutdown.
facts.claim: 2020 was a big exception: a large drop came despite new A/D line highs.

facts.quote: The handful of exceptions help to illustrate how there are no guarantees in the financial markets
facts.claim: The exceptions show there are no guarantees.

facts.quote: a few big cap stocks push the indices higher, but the rest of the market is not able to get enough oxygen to breathe, then that shows up in the A-D data.
facts.claim: When a few big caps lift the indexes while the rest of the market struggles, the A/D data show it.

facts.quote: This is what we saw all during 1999, and you probably remember what came after that period for the price indices.
facts.claim: McClellan says that narrow pattern ran all through 1999.

facts.quote: Market Capitalization-Based Weighting Reflects the economic significance of larger companies within the index.
facts.claim: The Nasdaq-100 is weighted by market cap, so larger companies count for more.

facts.quote: Equal Weighted Option Offers alternative investment through the Nasdaq-100 Equal Weighted™ Index to reduce concentration risk.
facts.claim: Nasdaq runs an equal-weighted Nasdaq-100 version to reduce concentration risk.

facts.quote: The S&P 500® Index is designed to measure the performance of the large-cap segment of the US equity market. It is float-adjusted market capitalization weighted.
facts.claim: The S&P 500 is weighted by float-adjusted market cap.

walkthroughs.title: Count the stocks, not the points
steps: Big indexes like the S&P 500 weight each stock by its market cap. The giants move the number most.
So an index can climb while more than half its stocks fall. A handful of big winners drags it up.
Breadth counts stocks instead. On the A/D line every stock gets one vote, big or small.
McClellan saw it all through 1999: a few big caps lifted the indexes while the A/D data showed the rest struggling.

walkthroughs.title: Confirm or diverge
steps: Each day, take the stocks that rose minus the ones that fell. That's net advances. The A/D line keeps a running total.
When the A/D line makes new highs with the index, the rally is broad. That's healthy.
Index at a new high, A/D line below its last peak: fewer stocks are doing the lifting. That's a bearish divergence.
A condition, not a signal. In 2007 the NYSE A/D line peaked in June. The index still hit new highs in October.

walkthroughs.title: Three more gauges
steps: Percent above the 50-day: the share of stocks above their 50-day average. Over 50% leans bullish, under 50% leans bearish.
New highs vs new lows: more stocks at 52-week highs than at 52-week lows favors the bulls.
It lags at turns. In 2009 the NYSE Composite bottomed in early March; net new highs didn't top +100 until August.
The McClellan Oscillator is the 19-day EMA of net advances minus the 39-day EMA. Above zero, advancing stocks have the upper hand.

questions.q: What does market breadth measure?
choices: How many stocks join a move
How far the index moved today
How big an order the market absorbs
How much volume traded today
questions.answer: How many stocks join a move
questions.why: How many stocks join a move. Breadth counts the stocks taking part in a trend, not the points the index gained.
questions.lesson_line: The index tells you how far. Breadth tells you how many came along.

wrong.How far the index moved today: That's the index's change. Breadth asks how many stocks went with it.
wrong.How big an order the market absorbs: That's market depth: how much size trades without moving the price much. A different idea.
wrong.How much volume traded today: That's volume. Some breadth gauges add volume, but breadth itself counts the stocks taking part.

questions.q: An index can close higher on a day when most of its stocks close lower.
questions.why: True. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 weight stocks by market cap. A few giants with big gains can lift the index while most of its stocks fall.
questions.lesson_line: Green index, red stocks. It happens, and breadth is how you catch it.

questions.q: What is the A/D line?
choices: A running total of net advances
Up volume minus down volume
New highs minus new lows
The index minus its 50-day average
questions.answer: A running total of net advances
questions.why: A running total of net advances. Each day's advancers minus decliners is added to the total from the day before.
questions.lesson_line: Net advances are one day. The A/D line is every day added up.

wrong.Up volume minus down volume: That's an up/down volume spread, a volume gauge. The A/D line counts stocks, not shares.
wrong.New highs minus new lows: That's net new highs, a different breadth gauge.
wrong.The index minus its 50-day average: That's a price reading on one chart. The A/D line counts how many stocks rose and fell.

questions.q: A $2 trillion company and a $2 billion company both close up today. How does each count on the A/D line?
choices: The same: just one advance each
The giant counts for far more
By how much each one rose
By how many shares each traded
questions.answer: The same: just one advance each
questions.why: The same: one advance each. Market cap and volume don't matter. An advance counts +1 and a decline counts -1.
questions.lesson_line: On the A/D line, every stock gets one vote.

wrong.The giant counts for far more: That's how a cap-weighted index counts. The A/D line ignores size on purpose.
wrong.By how much each one rose: A tiny gain and a huge gain both count as one advance.
wrong.By how many shares each traded: Volume doesn't enter the A/D line. Volume-based breadth gauges are separate tools.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The standard net new highs count subtracts stocks at new ___-week lows from those at new highs.
questions.why: 52. New highs and new lows are stocks at their highest or lowest price of the past 52 weeks.
questions.lesson_line: The classic new highs and new lows count is built on 52-week highs and lows.

questions.q: On the A/D line, the actual number matters more than its shape and direction.
questions.why: False. The number depends on the day you start counting. ChartSchool says to read the shape and direction, and McClellan says the scale isn't important.
questions.lesson_line: Read the A/D line's trend, its highs and its lows. Ignore its level.

questions.q: The index makes a higher high. The A/D line makes a lower high. What is this called?
choices: Bearish divergence
Bullish divergence
Breadth confirmation
Breadth thrust
questions.why: Bearish divergence. The index is rising on fewer stocks, so participation is narrowing.
questions.lesson_line: Higher high in price, lower high in breadth: fewer stocks are carrying it.

wrong.Bullish divergence: That's the mirror image at a low: the index makes a lower low and the A/D line a higher low.
wrong.Breadth confirmation: Confirmation is the A/D line making new highs with the index. Here it fell short.
wrong.Breadth thrust: A thrust is a fast surge in advancing stocks, usually off a low. Nothing here is surging.

questions.q: What is the McClellan Oscillator built from?
choices: Two averages of net advances
Two averages of the index price
New highs minus new lows
Up volume divided by down volume
questions.why: Two averages of net advances. It's the 19-day EMA of net advances minus the 39-day EMA. Sherman and Marian McClellan created it in 1969.
questions.lesson_line: The McClellan Oscillator is momentum for breadth, not for price.

wrong.Two averages of the index price: That's MACD on price. The McClellan Oscillator works like MACD, but on net advances.
wrong.New highs minus new lows: That's net new highs, a separate breadth gauge.
wrong.Up volume divided by down volume: That's a volume ratio. The McClellan Oscillator counts advancing and declining stocks.

questions.q: On the NYSE today, 2,140 stocks rose and 1,060 fell. What were net advances?
questions.why: 1,080. Advancers minus decliners: 2,140 less 1,060. A positive day adds to the A/D line.
questions.lesson_line: More stocks up than down, the A/D line rises. More down than up, it falls.

questions.q: The A/D line read 15,200 yesterday. Today 1,250 stocks rose and 1,900 fell. Where does the A/D line stand now?
questions.why: 14,550. Today's net advances were negative, so the line falls from 15,200 by that amount.
questions.lesson_line: Yesterday's line plus today's net advances. That's the whole math.

questions.q: The NYSE A/D line mostly tells you how the biggest companies are doing.
questions.why: False. Every stock counts the same, and most listed stocks are small and mid caps. The A/D line tracks the average stock, not the giants.
questions.lesson_line: The index shows the giants. The A/D line shows the average stock.

questions.q: The share of stocks above their 50-day average swings more than the share above their 200-day.
questions.why: True. The 50-day version is more volatile and crosses 50% more often. It suits short swings; the 150-day and 200-day suit the longer trend.
questions.lesson_line: 50-day breadth for the swing, 200-day breadth for the big trend.

questions.q: In a 500-stock index, 120 stocks close above their 50-day average. What percent of the index is that?
questions.why: 24%. Stocks above the average divided by all stocks in the index. Under 50% gives breadth a bearish bias.
questions.lesson_line: Over 50% above the 50-day leans bullish. Under 50% leans bearish.

questions.q: Today 60 stocks hit new 52-week highs and 140 hit new 52-week lows. What percent of that total are new highs?
questions.why: 30%. New highs divided by new highs plus new lows, times 100. ChartSchool calls it the Record High Percent. Below 50, new lows outnumber new highs.
questions.lesson_line: Below 50, new lows rule the day. That leans bearish.

questions.q: The 19-day EMA of net advances is +150. The 39-day EMA is +60. What is the McClellan Oscillator?
questions.why: 90. The 19-day EMA minus the 39-day EMA. It's positive, so advancing stocks have the upper hand.
questions.lesson_line: Above zero, breadth momentum favors the bulls. Below zero, the bears.

questions.story: The S&P 500 closes at a record high. Its A/D line is still below the peak it set two months ago. Fewer stocks are above their 50-day average than at that peak.
questions.q: What is breadth telling you?
choices: Fewer stocks are carrying the rally
Breadth confirms the new record high
The top is in, so sell everything
questions.answer: Fewer stocks are carrying the rally
questions.why: Fewer stocks are carrying the rally. The index made a new high without the A/D line. That's narrowing participation: a warning to respect, not a sell order.
questions.lesson_line: A new high on fewer stocks is a warning. Price still has to confirm it.

wrong.Breadth confirms the new record high: Confirmation needs the A/D line at a new high too. It's still below its last peak.
wrong.The top is in, so sell everything: A divergence is a condition, not a signal. A lot of bullish new highs can come before the last one, so watch price for a break of support.

questions.story: The index breaks below last month's low. This time the A/D line holds above its own low from last month.
questions.q: What's the best read?
choices: Fewer stocks falling; watch price
The selling is broad and speeding up
The bottom is in, so buy with size
questions.why: Fewer stocks are falling with it. Lower low in the index, higher low in the A/D line: that's a bullish divergence. Let price confirm the turn before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Breadth can show the selling drying up. Price tells you when to act.

wrong.The selling is broad and speeding up: Broad selling would drag the A/D line to a new low too. It held above its last low.
wrong.The bottom is in, so buy with size: A bullish divergence says the decline may be ending. It isn't a buy signal on its own.

questions.q: The McClellan Oscillator jumps from -75 to +60 within a week. How many points did it climb?
questions.why: 135 points. On the McClellan Oscillator, a big move from negative to positive, typically 100 points or more, is called a breadth thrust. ChartSchool's typical one runs from below -50 to above +50.
questions.lesson_line: Most important lows show a sharp surge in breadth. Not every surge starts a big run.

questions.story: After a sharp drop, only 12% of S&P 500 stocks are above their 50-day average. The index is still making lower lows.
questions.q: What's your plan?
choices: Wait for breadth and price to turn up
Buy now; it can't get more oversold
Press shorts; breadth is collapsing
questions.answer: Wait for breadth and price to turn up
questions.why: Wait for the turn. ChartSchool counts below 30% as oversold, but oversold is not a buy signal on its own. In a strong downtrend this gauge can go oversold again and again.
questions.lesson_line: Oversold tells you where you are, not when it turns. Wait for the upturn.

wrong.Buy now; it can't get more oversold: It can. In a strong downtrend this gauge can stay oversold many times over. ChartSchool says wait for an upturn.
wrong.Press shorts; breadth is collapsing: Selling into an oversold extreme is late. In ChartSchool's downtrend example, the selling alerts came on overbought bounces.

questions.story: Early June 2007: the NYSE A/D line peaks. The NYSE Composite still makes new highs in July and October. Then the 2008 bear market begins.
questions.q: What does this case teach about breadth divergences?
choices: They can warn months before a top
They mark the exact day of the top
They only show up after the top
questions.answer: They can warn months before a top
questions.why: They can warn months early. McClellan dates the A/D peak to June 4, 2007, just over 4 months before the Dow's final top.
questions.lesson_line: A divergence is a warning with no clock on it. Price tells you when.

wrong.They mark the exact day of the top: The A/D line peaked in June and the index still made new highs in October. Breadth gauges are poor timing tools.
wrong.They only show up after the top: Here breadth turned first, months before the index did.

questions.story: The index has been in a strong uptrend all year. The share of its stocks above their 50-day average has topped 70% several times.
questions.q: What do those repeated high readings tell you?
choices: Breadth is strong, not topping
It's overbought, so go short now
The uptrend is about to end soon
questions.why: Breadth is strong. ChartSchool calls above 70% overbought, but in a strong uptrend this gauge can go overbought again and again. Multiple overbought readings are a sign of strength.
questions.lesson_line: In an uptrend, overbought breadth is strength. Dips to oversold that turn back up are the chances.

wrong.It's overbought, so go short now: In ChartSchool's uptrend example, overbought readings were ignored. Shorting strength fights the trend.
wrong.The uptrend is about to end soon: Strong trends can hold breadth gauges at extremes for a long time. A high reading alone doesn't end a trend.

questions.story: Mid-April 2026. The S&P 500 is back above 7,000 after a sharp selloff. Its A/D line has climbed with it since the late-March low.
questions.q: How does breadth grade this rally?
choices: Broad: many stocks are joining in
Narrow: a few giants carry it up
Bearish: breadth is now diverging
questions.answer: Broad: many stocks are joining in
questions.why: Broad. The A/D line is rising with the index, which shows wide participation. Fidelity read that combination as broadly bullish.
questions.lesson_line: Index and A/D line rising together is the healthy picture.

wrong.Narrow: a few giants carry it up: Narrow means the index rises while the A/D line lags. Here the A/D line rose with it.
wrong.Bearish: breadth is now diverging: A divergence needs the two to split. They climbed together.

questions.story: June 2024. The Nasdaq Composite is making new all-time highs. Its A/D line sits near its all-time low.
questions.q: What's the best read?
choices: A known Nasdaq quirk, not a crash call
The Nasdaq rally is a false one
A crash is coming in a few weeks
questions.answer: A known Nasdaq quirk, not a crash call
questions.why: A known quirk. Nasdaq listing standards are looser, so stocks that fail keep piling into the declines column. Its A/D line can fall for long stretches while the index rises.
questions.lesson_line: Don't read the Nasdaq A/D line like the NYSE's. It can drift down even in bull markets.

wrong.The Nasdaq rally is a false one: The index really made new highs. The A/D line's slide comes largely from failing small listings, not from the leaders.
wrong.A crash is coming in a few weeks: McClellan noted the Nasdaq A/D line has never got back to where its data began in 1972. A drift that old says little about the next few weeks.

questions.story: December 2013. The Dow makes a new high, but the NYSE A/D line is still below its October 29 peak. By June 2014 it is making higher highs again.
questions.q: What did that divergence turn out to be?
choices: A warning that went away
A sell signal for a bear market
Proof the A/D line has stopped working
questions.why: A warning that went away. When the A/D line goes on to new highs, the divergence is repaired. That's why McClellan calls a divergence a condition, not a signal.
questions.lesson_line: Respect a divergence, then keep checking. Breadth can repair it.

wrong.A sell signal for a bear market: By June 2014 breadth was making new highs again. McClellan read that as liquidity lifting the majority of issues.
wrong.Proof the A/D line has stopped working: One warning that fades doesn't break the tool. The same kind of divergence came months before the 2007 top.

questions.q: A new high in the NYSE A/D line rules out a big market drop over the next three months.
questions.why: False. It's good news, and McClellan's study found the drop after one was usually about 10% at most. But 2011 brought a 19% drop anyway, and 2020 was another big exception.
questions.lesson_line: Strong breadth tilts the odds. It never removes the risk. Keep your stops.

questions.story: Your breakout setup triggers. The index sits near its high, but its A/D line has slid for six weeks. For two weeks, new 52-week lows have outnumbered new highs.
questions.q: Which plan fits this breadth?
choices: Pass: breadth favors the bears now
Buy full size; the index is strong
Short the index right now
questions.answer: Pass: breadth favors the bears now
questions.why: Pass. With new lows outnumbering new highs, breadth gives a bearish bias. ChartSchool's approach then is to favor bearish signals and set bullish ones aside.
questions.lesson_line: Breadth sets the bias. Price gives the trigger. Against the bias, I'd rather pass.

wrong.Buy full size; the index is strong: The index leans on its giants. The A/D line and the new lows say most stocks are weakening.
wrong.Short the index right now: Breadth is a bias, not a trigger. The index hasn't broken anything yet, so there's no short signal.

conflicts: McClellan Summation Index neutral level: McClellan Financial Publications (s14) says the properly calibrated Summation Index 'is neutral at the +1000 level', while ChartSchool's Summation Index page (https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-indicators/mcclellan-summation-index) calls it an oscillator that 'fluctuates above and below the zero line'. The two use different calculations. No question asks about the Summation Index's level.

McClellan Oscillator versions: the classic version uses NYSE net advances (s14, s15); StockCharts' version is ratio-adjusted (net advances divided by advances plus declines, times 1000) and Investopedia shows both. Their values differ, and McClellan (s16) notes A-D numbers differ from one data source to the next. Every oscillator question gives its own EMA or oscillator values and keys only the 19-minus-39 structure and the sign. Investopedia's first EMA formula as printed omits subtracting the prior EMA; it is not used.

Overbought and oversold levels: ChartSchool uses 70% / 30% for the share of stocks above the 50-day and says 'These levels may vary for other indices'; Investopedia uses 30 / 70 for the new highs-lows index. No question keys a threshold as a rule: q19 and q21 name 70% and 30% as ChartSchool's levels.

Breadth thrust has two definitions: the McClellan Oscillator thrust (ChartSchool: from below -50 to above +50; Investopedia: 100 points or more from negative to positive), and Martin Zweig's breadth thrust (10-day EMA of advances / (advances + declines) going from below 0.40 to above 0.615 within 10 days; Investopedia's breadth-thrust page and McClellan's July 1, 2011 Chart In Focus agree on it). q18 names the McClellan Oscillator version only. Zweig's version and its count of past signals are not quizzed.
Fidelity (s13) calls the A/D line a sentiment indicator; ChartSchool (s1) files it under breadth and keeps sentiment indicators separate. The unit calls it breadth.

Investopedia's High-Low Index page says the index is bullish 'if it is positive and rising, and bearish if it is negative and falling', but the same page defines it as a 0-100 percent average read against 50. The unit uses only the 50 line, which ChartSchool and Investopedia both state.

McClellan's research claims (major tops have typically followed A-D line divergences by 3 to 6 months; after a new A-D line high the next 3-month drawdown is usually about 10% or less) are one analyst's studies. They are never keyed as fact; q25 names the 10% figure as McClellan's study and keys only the exceptions he lists (2011, 2020).

The new-highs lag (ChartSchool: the market turns 'one to three months before' new highs and lows shift; the 2009 example) is from one publisher only, so it is taught in walk-through w3 and never keyed in a question.

Track audit 2026-11-09: F7.04 q14 keys a breadth thrust by its general meaning and names Zweig's version in its why; q18 here now names the McClellan Oscillator version in its why, so each definition carries its name.
